messages.subject: Re: Using SECR to inform future sampling.
messages.subject_clean: Using SECR to inform future sampling.
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rudy

Welcome to the group. I'm afraid SECR probably doesn't offer you much. As I understand it, you are thinking about mapping differential use within a home range.as <http://range.as> a guide to future sampling for some other purpose. SECR tends to assume individual home ranges are circular and proceed from there to estimate population-level parameters, particularly density. The circular assumption is fairly innocuous when we  only care about population density. Technically one _can_ model irregular ranges that conform to habitat covariate(s) - see Royle, J.A., Chandler, R.B., Sun, C.C.& Fuller, A.K. (2013) Integrating resource selection information with spatial capture–recapture. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 4, 520–530 - probably a laborious and data-greedy approach to your particular problem.

I suppose even a circular home-range model might be of some use to limit a search area if you wanted to resample particular individuals, but I'm lost without a clearer idea of your mission.

Murray

messages.subject: Issue modeling finite mixtures when using user-defined non-Euclidean detection function
messages.subject_clean: Issue modeling finite mixtures when using user-defined non-Euclidean detection function
messages.body_plain:
Hello Murray et al.,

I have a Peromyscus sp. capture-recapture dataset comprised of 33 individuals that were detected 80 times over 5 occasions. The sampling occurred on 3 grids of 100 traps each, located along the bottom of a linearly oriented northwest to southeast canyon (azimuth of approximately 105 degrees). Thus, I have reason to believe that the base assumption of Euclidean detection/movement (i.e., bivariate normal or isotropic) is not appropriate for this system.

Indeed, I used the user-defined non-Euclidean (anisotropic) detection function that we previously developed (see Murphy et al. 2016. J. Wild. Mgmt. 80:1390-1407) in a null model (D~1, g0~1, sigma~1) and compared that to the same null model with an isotropic detection function; the anisotropic model had an AICc value that was 10 units lower than the isotropic model. Clearly, the anisotropic detection functions should be used. As an aside, habitat and elevation where the grids were located were relatively homogeneous, so using Royle's LCP ecological distance won't work.

Nonetheless, I need to consider sex-specific detection and movement to account for potential heterogeneity. However, when I model the 2-class finite mixtures (h2) on g0 or sigma, with hcov = "Sex", in combination with my anisotropic detection function, the models do not run. Below is the error that I keep getting from R:

> mod1a=secr.fit (alldata, hcov = "Sex", model=list(D~1, g0~h2, sigma~1), mask = maskCovs,details=list(userdist=mydistfn),
+                link = list(noneuc = 'log'), start = list(noneuc =exp(-0.4)))
Checking data
Preparing detection design matrices
Preparing density design matrix
Preparing non-Euclidean parameter design matrix
Finding initial parameter values...
Initial values  D = 3.34721, g0 = 0.01704, sigma = 47.10141
Maximizing likelihood...
Eval     Loglik        D       g0   g0.h2M    sigma pmix.h2M   noneuc
Error in (function (f, p, ..., hessian = FALSE, typsize = rep(1, length(p)),  :
  missing value in parameter

I initially thought that this was either an issue with the starting value or with maximization, so I tried numerous different starting values ranging from exp(-4) to exp (4), but continuously received the same error. I then used the OVpossum example provided in the non-Euclidean vignette and added h2 to g0; the same error was received:

datadir <-  system.file(  "extdata"  ,  package =    "secr")
ovforest <- rgdal::  readOGR(  dsn =    paste0  (datadir,    "/OVforest.shp"  ),  layer =    "OVforest")
eftbank <-  read.table(  paste0 (datadir,    "/leftbank.txt"  ))[    21    :      195    ,]# for plotting
ovposs <- OVpossumCH[[  1  ]]# February 1996
ovmask <-  make.mask(  traps  (ovposs),  buffer =    120  ,  type =    "trapbuffer"  ,  poly =    ovforest[1: 2 ,],  spacing =    7.5  ,  keep.poly =    FALSE)

fn1 <- function (xy1, xy2, mask) {
  if (    missing    (xy1))    return  (    "noneuc"  )
  sig <-    covariates  (mask)$noneuc  # sigma(x,y) at mask points
  sig <-    matrix  (sig,    byrow =      TRUE    ,    nrow =      nrow    (xy1),    ncol =      nrow    (xy2))
  euc <-    edist  (xy1, xy2)
  euc / sig
  }
fit1 <-  secr.fit(ovposs,  model=list(D~1, g0~h2, sigma~1,noneuc ~ x + y + x2 + y2 + xy),mask = ovmask ,  trace = FALSE  ,  details =  list(userdist = fn1),  fixed =list(sigma =1  ))

Thus, there appears to be a bug in secr (v3.0.1) that prevents non-Euclidean detection functions from being used with h2 mixtures. Has anyone had a similar issue or know of a way to resolve this issue?

Thanks,

Sean

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I am an honors student teaching myself secr with the goal of estimating seasonal variation in home range overlap in my study species (voles). I plan to measure overlap as the number of territories that intersect each grid cell (but please tell me if there is a better method). My data were taken from a 7x7 grid and I am using conditional likelihood secr models with an exponential detection function. I believe I know how to map each individual animal’s 95% contour using the following:

#session 2, 30 individuals

fxiout <- fxi.contour (model01, 1:30, sessnum = 2, plt = FALSE, fitmode = TRUE)

t(sapply(fxiout, "[[", "mode"))

## using fill colours

## lty = 0 suppresses contour lines

## nx = 256 ensures smooth outline

plot(traps(captures_all))

fxi.contour(model01, 1:30, sessnum = 2, add = TRUE, p = 0.95,

            drawlabels = FALSE, nx = 256, fill = topo.colors(4), lty = 0)

Assuming my code is correct (in reality I only examine two animals at a time otherwise it’s too cluttered), is the plotted 95% contour level of probability the same as the HR95, or do I need to make additional calculations?

Also, when is it appropriate to convert the data to a spatial polygon data frame? I believe I have the correct code for this as well but can’t figure out how to overlay the trapping grid to examine overlap.

## output as SpatialPolygonsDataFrame

spdf <- fxi.contour(model01, 1:30,sessnum = 2, plt = FALSE, p = 0.95,

                    nx = 256, SPDF = TRUE, fitmode = TRUE)

## save as ESRI shapefile

library(maptools)

writeSpatialShape(spdf, fn = "hranges")

## plot contours and modes

plot(spdf)

points(data.frame(spdf))

#Plot each animal one at a time

plot(spdf[1,])

Any insight would be greatly appreciated.

messages.subject: Re: Correct method for measuring home range overlap?
messages.subject_clean: Correct method for measuring home range overlap?
messages.body_plain:
Hello Hansen

I think you're heading down the wrong path. The contours from fxi.xxx bear no relation to contours of home-range utilization. This misunderstanding also underlies the common misuse of the pooled fxi surface as a map of density. The fxi contours change with sampling effort, as you can see by simulating some data and then doubling the number of occasions.

The index k = sqrt(D).sigma gives some insight into overlap, and you might check out how it varies seasonally (I predict: a lot). Interpretation of k as 'overlap' assumes a constant spatial dispersion (e.g. 2-D Poisson) and requires you to stick to one detection function (usually halfnormal for comparability between studies). Modelling D & k (= 'sigmak' in secr) instead of D and sigma can be informative. You might also check Ecography 39:676.

Cheers
Murray

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have mark-recapture data for a rare canid species. The traps are organized across the landscape in clusters of 6 traps and are far enough apart that we don’t capture the same individuals between clusters. Each cluster of traps has similar geometry in terms of the trap lay-out. We only have a few captures and re-captures in each cluster since this is a wide-ranging and rare species. We are hoping to use density estimates from secr to help us estimate total abundance of this species.

I originally considered treating each cluster as a separate session since they are spatially independent but I no longer think that will work because the data is so sparse (and therefore it won’t be possible to parameterize the detection function for each session). However, in reading through the secr-overview it seems that using a detector cluster approach might be appropriate.

With that in mind, I’m hoping someone can help shed some light on the following:
Firstly, does using a detector cluster approach for this make sense (rather than separate sessions)?

I tried the detector cluster approach using a modified version of the example snowshoe hare data and noticed that it results in only one overall density output rather than a separate density estimate for each cluster. Is there any way to extract density estimates for each cluster? I see from the derived.cluster() help file that each cluster is interpreted as a replicate sample, and am hoping that there is some way to pull out the results for each of those replicates.

If the program doesn’t produce individual density estimates for each cluster, would it be appropriate to compile all capture/re-capture data and pretend like they are all from one detector cluster for the purposes of generating an ‘general esa’ and then subsequently calculating density for each cluster by dividing the # of different individuals captured by the general esa?

If I should have been able to extract separate density estimates for each cluster, perhaps I added the cluster attribute incorrectly. If this is the case, any insights or examples on how to add the cluster attribute to traps data would be much appreciated. At the moment I am adding the ClusterID attribute after the traps object is created by assigning a vector to clusterID(traps).

Many thanks in advance for your help!

Hi All,

I am Iding, currently doing camera trapping field work in a Sumatran rainforest. I have four study areas that each comprises of ~ paired camera trap stations. My aims is to estimate density of clouded leopard and further species interaction, temporal and spatial.

I realized that although with enormous effort that doubled or even quadrupled, I found little capture and recapture of targeted animal: the Sumatran clouded leopard. I detected individuals 3-5, from each study areas. Encouragingly, I detected female cloudie in each study area (session) but not surprisingly, I got very few detection.

For the models, I have ran constant model that estimate cloudie density across study area as a single population. I therefore would like to focus on how to:
estimate density of cloudie in each session as independent location as each has >60-80 km apart.
include sex as covariate and see if density between male and female is different.
estimate sex ratio considered that I have very limited female detection.
For the analyses, I have been assisted by Mike Meredith but the more I read, the more I am confused.

I really appreciate if you could spare your time and thoughts on this matter.

Cheers,
Iding

Dear Iding
Thanks for your enquiry. I hate to say this, but I do not think you can conduct a meaningful capture-recapture analysis of such a sparse dataset. I know there are many instances of capture-recapture methods being applied to very sparse datasets, but I think we have to be clear that this is undesirable. Your hard-won data may have to stand on their own without statistics, or at most provide a single pooled estimate of density.
Regards
Murray

messages.body_plain:
Hello. I am very new to SECR. I have perused the previous inquiries in this Google Group, however, I could not find a clear answer to my question so I thought I'd ask. I am estimating density and abundance of forest elephants and I want to model differences in detection probability as well as sex differences. While I think I know how to generate a null model and examine sex differences in detection (see below) I am unsure of how to look at differences in detection probability (other than sex as a factor). Any insight would be very much appreciated. Thank you very much.

- Colin M. Brand

Null Model:
m1 <- secr.fit (Ele, detectfn = 'EX', model = list(D~1, g0~1, sigma~1), buffer = 2000)

Sex Differences:
m2 <- secr.fit (Ele, detectfn = 'EX', model = list(D~1, g0~h2, sigma~h2), buffer = 2000, hcov = "Sex")

I am using such a small buffer because nearly all of the study area is surrounded by water.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm trying to make a mask because my data was collected on islands and thus has defined limits, but I'm running into some problems.

I made a polygon using the sp package, where the projected coordinates were points outlining the islands shape:

> Gx <- Gooseberry_projected_coordinates$x
> Gy <- Gooseberry_projected_coordinates$y
> Gxy = cbind(Gx, Gy)
> Gxy
> Gpolygon1 <- Polygon(Gxy)
> plot(Gxy)

I have attached the polygon because I don't think I made it correctly - the points are not joined and this may be the cause of the problem in making the mask.

I then tried to make a mask to include in my SECR model (where GRat traps is the capthist of my trap and capt files i.e.
GRat <- read.capthist("Gooseberry Capt.txt", "Gooseberry Trap.txt", detector = "single", skip = 1))

However I have come up with the following error and I don't know why:
> GMask <- make.mask(traps(GRat), buffer=5, type="polygon", poly = Gpolygon)
Error in as.vector(data) :
  no method for coercing this S4 class to a vector

Could anyone help me understand what I've done wrong?

Cheers,

Annabel
